source.title_on_document: How AI Ideas Affect the Creativity, Diversity, and Evolution of Human Ideas: Evidence From a Large, Dynamic Experiment

supplement.where: Appendices A-D (pp. 13-16) and Section E, Supplementary Information SI 1-SI 11 (pp. 17-29), inside this PDF
supplement.holds: Regression tables with SEs and t statistics for creativity (Table 18, p. 26), local idea diversity (Table 14, p. 23), evolution of idea diversity (Table 17, p. 25), and AI adoption (Table 22, p. 28); global-diversity contrasts for all three metrics (Tables 11-13, pp. 21-22); moderator contrasts (Tables 15-16, 19-21); moderator selection (Table 10, SI 7); exclusions (SI 3, pp. 17-18); ChatGPT-vs-human originality (SI 4, Table 6, p. 19); sample characteristics (SI 6, p. 20). The per-arm creativity coefficients and all local-diversity results appear only here; the main text gives the joint creativity F test, Cliff's deltas for the global-diversity contrasts with Control, and the high-exposure evolution slopes.

paper_design_summary: Online volunteers recruited through Reddit, Facebook ads, and the Creative Mornings newsletter (844 people analyzed) each completed up to five Alternate Uses Task trials in a randomized sequence, one trial per condition, after a landing page told everyone they would see ideas from prior participants and from ChatGPT. In each trial they ranked six example ideas and then wrote their own: the control showed six human ideas from prior participants in the same condition and item, and four AI conditions replaced two (low exposure) or four (high exposure) of them with pre-generated ChatGPT-3.5 ideas, labeled or not labeled as AI (disclosure). Each submitted idea was scored for originality by a fine-tuned GPT-3 classifier, and SBERT embedding distances measured diversity among the ideas in a condition (global), its change over trials (evolution), distance from the examples seen (local), and similarity to the AI examples (AI adoption).

studies.label: Dynamic online AUT experiment (AI exposure x disclosure, response chains)

assignment.what_was_assigned: A sequence of five (item, condition) trials. Each AUT item (tire, pants, shoe, table, bottle) is mapped to one of five conditions so that neither items nor conditions repeat within a person's sequence. Conditions: Control (0 AI, 6 human examples); Low Exposure (2 AI, 4 human) and High Exposure (4 AI, 2 human), each with the AI ideas labeled as AI (Disclosed) or not (Undisclosed).
assignment.quote: Participants are randomized to a sequence of 5 trials. In each trial, participants generate a creative use for an item under a specific experimental condition. Neither items nor conditions repeat in a 5-trial sequence.
assignment.locator: p. 5, Figure 2 caption and Section 3.4.2 (Randomization); conditions in p. 2, Figure 1

arms.name: Control
arms.description: Six human example ideas: the most recent ideas from prior participants in the same condition-item response chain, with Organisciak-dataset seeds early in a chain; no AI ideas; Disclosure = No. No example carries a source label, although the landing page had told every participant that some examples would come from ChatGPT (p. 5, Figure 3).

arms.name: Low Exposure, Undisclosed
arms.description: 2 ChatGPT ideas + 4 human ideas; AI ideas not labeled. No example carries a source label, although the landing page had told every participant that some examples would come from ChatGPT (p. 5, Figure 3).

arms.name: Low Exposure, Disclosed
arms.description: 2 ChatGPT ideas + 4 human ideas; AI ideas labeled as AI

arms.name: High Exposure, Undisclosed
arms.description: 4 ChatGPT ideas + 2 human ideas; AI ideas not labeled. No example carries a source label, although the landing page had told every participant that some examples would come from ChatGPT (p. 5, Figure 3).

arms.name: High Exposure, Disclosed
arms.description: 4 ChatGPT ideas + 2 human ideas; AI ideas labeled as AI

participants.exclusions: Only participants who completed at least one trial are analyzed; the number who consented without completing a trial is not stated. Two responses shown in error and 36 profane responses were removed, leaving 3,414 of 3,452 responses (SI 3, pp. 17-18). Four implausible ages were set to missing and the responses kept. Participants averaged 4.05 responses (Table 2). The creativity and local-diversity models report 3,271 observations (Tables 18, 14) and the AI-adoption model, defined only in the four AI conditions, 2,618 (Table 22); the paper does not explain the gap from 3,414. Per-condition counts of people or responses are not reported.
participants.who: Unpaid adult volunteers (verified 18 or older) recruited through the Creative Mornings newsletter (343, 40.6%), r/InternetIsBeautiful (298, 35.3%), r/samplesize (94), share links (61), other subreddits, and Facebook ads (Table 3). The paper describes the sample as creative professionals and technology-oriented users. Mean age 34.92 (SD 10.86); among non-missing responses 50% women, 43% men (p. 7).
participants.country: 48 countries; top five by responses (77.85% of responses): United States, Canada, Germany, United Kingdom, Australia (SI 6, p. 20)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-3.5 (zero-shot prompt adapted from Stevenson et al., with an added instruction to match the mean human word count)
ai_tool.how_used: In the four AI conditions, two (Low Exposure) or four (High Exposure) randomly drawn, pre-generated ChatGPT AUT ideas took the place of human ideas among the six example ideas shown in the trial. Control trials showed six human ideas (p. 2, Figure 1). Participants ranked the examples by creativity and then wrote their own idea on the same screen. They did not interact with the model, and the paper calls this passive exposure. But the landing page told every participant that they would see ideas 'even from AI (i.e., ChatGPT)' and would rank them (p. 5, Figure 3), and the paper added the ranking task 'to ensure engagement with the example ideas' (p. 5, Section 3.4.3). So the Undisclosed conditions omit the per-idea source labels. They do not hide that the study showed AI ideas. In Disclosed conditions each AI example carried a '(Source: A.I)' label and each human example a '(Source: Human)' label, and the Disclosed screen in Figure 12 also shows the banner 'For this object, we also asked AI to come up with ideas!' (p. 4, Section 3.2; p. 16, Figure 12).

task.description: Alternate Uses Task variant: after ranking six example ideas, submit one creative use for an everyday item (tire, pants, shoe, table, or bottle). Each submitted idea becomes an example for later participants in the same condition-item response chain; chains reset every 20 trials, with 7 chains per condition-item (175 chains, 3,500 targeted responses).
task.duration: Study described to participants as taking 3-6 minutes (Figure 3, p. 5); average 144.31 seconds per response (Table 2, p. 7)

outcomes.name: Individual creativity: predicted originality of the submitted idea
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Prediction from the fine-tuned GPT-3 Davinci classifier of Organisciak et al., trained on human creativity ratings normalized to 1-5 (r = 0.81 with human judgments of AUT originality overall; r = 0.88-0.91 for the five items used; p. 3, Section 1.2.1; p. 4, Section 3.2; p. 13, A.1). The paper calls the score creativity but states that it measures originality. Linear mixed model with crossed random intercepts for participant and for response chain nested in item-condition, controlling for self-perceived creativity, AI-relative creativity, interest group, trial number, AI feeling, condition order, log duration, and number of seeds (Table 18); joint F test of condition via emmeans (p. 8). No moderator interactions were retained for creativity (Table 10, p. 21). Per-arm means and SDs are not printed. The trial-number slope test is a separate outcome (S1-O2).

outcomes.name: Global idea diversity: median pairwise distance among submitted ideas in a condition
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Median pairwise SBERT cosine distance (x100) among 50 submitted ideas sampled per condition-item, repeated over 50 Monte Carlo runs, using only ideas submitted after the sixth trial of a response chain (p. 15, B.2; p. 21, SI 8.1). Robustness: mean pairwise distance (Table 11, p. 21) and mean distance to the centroid (Table 13, p. 22), described as directionally similar (p. 8). Condition-level values with 95% CI error bars appear only in Figure 7 (p. 7). Higher = more diverse, so no sign reversal is needed. Tables 11-13 also print High-versus-Low exposure contrasts across disclosure levels (rows 6 and 7). They change exposure and disclosure at once and are not coded.

diversity_detail.metric: Median pairwise cosine distance between SBERT embeddings, scaled by 100; robustness: mean pairwise distance and mean distance to the set centroid
diversity_detail.embedding_model: SBERT (Sentence-BERT); the specific checkpoint is not named
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs within a random sample of 50 submitted ideas per condition-item combination, repeated for 50 Monte Carlo runs; only ideas submitted after the sixth trial of a response chain
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Two-tailed paired permutation tests (10,000 iterations), paired on Monte Carlo seed and item, with 1 added to numerator and denominator and a Holm-Bonferroni adjustment; Cliff's delta as effect size. No standard errors and no participant-level uncertainty.
diversity_detail.notes: Compares ideas from different participants within a condition. Ideas within a response chain are not independent, because each participant sees prior participants' ideas. Figure 7 (p. 7) shows condition-level values with 95% CIs only graphically. Locators: pp. 14-15, Appendix B.2; p. 21, SI 8.1.

outcomes.name: Local idea diversity: distance between a participant's idea and the example ideas that participant saw
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Median pairwise SBERT cosine distance (x100) between the submitted idea and the example ideas shown (Table 1, p. 7; SI 8.2, p. 23). Robustness: mean pairwise distance and distance to the examples' centroid (Table 14, models 2-3). Coded other because it compares one person's idea with the stimuli (prior participants' ideas, seeds, and AI ideas), not different people's outputs with each other. The model includes condition x self-perceived-creativity and condition x AI-relative-creativity interactions (Table 14; Table 10, p. 21), so the printed condition coefficients are effects at moderator values of zero; the paper does not say whether the moderators were centered. Reported only in the SI. Table 1 cites SI 8.3 for this measure; it is in SI 8.2.

outcomes.name: AI adoption: maximum similarity of the submitted idea to the AI examples shown
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Maximum SBERT cosine similarity (x100) between the submitted idea and the AI example ideas seen; robustness: mean and median similarity (Table 22, models 2-3). Defined only in the four AI conditions, so every contrast compares AI configurations and none compares with Control. The paper calls it a secondary outcome (p. 8) and does not interpret the main effect of condition because maximum similarity rises with the number of AI examples (p. 27). It measures convergence toward the AI examples, not creativity or diversity across people. Coded question with_ai by the codebook rule for an outcome produced with AI available whose construct is not diversity (codebook section 1; form-spec field note on question), as for S1-O5. The form-spec keeps none for outcomes that answer none of the three questions, such as AI output compared with human output. This outcome is scored on ideas that people wrote with AI examples on screen. Table 1 (p. 7) describes it as the 'maximum semantic distance', but Sections 1.2.2 and 5.5 and SI 10 define it as maximum cosine similarity.

company_involvement.description: None stated. The authors are at the University of Michigan and the University of Maryland (p. 1). Creative Mornings, described as an organization for creative professionals, agreed to distribute the study link (p. 4, Section 3.3). The acknowledgments thank colleagues for feedback, and no funding statement appears (p. 11).

eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 (met): S1 randomizes each participant to a sequence of five (item, condition) trials in which conditions do not repeat and their order is randomized (p. 5, Figure 2 and Section 3.4.2). Exposure to pre-generated ChatGPT example ideas (ideas_supplied) therefore varies within person, and the Control trial shows only human examples. Criterion 2 (met): 844 unique participants are analyzed (p. 7, Table 2), far above 50. The paper reports no per-arm counts, and participants completed 4.05 of 5 trials on average. The models print observations, not people (3,271 in Tables 14 and 18), and 11 participants lack the AI-feeling covariate (p. 20, Table 9). With at most one trial per condition per person, the models still hold at least 655 people. Criterion 3 (met): every outcome is scored on the submitted idea, by classifier-predicted originality and by SBERT diversity across people (p. 3; pp. 7-8). Caveats: the AI help is exposure to example ideas, not interaction with a chatbot. The landing page told every participant that some examples came from ChatGPT (p. 5, Figure 3), so disclosure varies only the per-idea labels. Unless Control comes first in the sequence, a participant's Control trial follows AI trials on other items. Ideas within response chains are not independent, and the diversity results carry no participant-level uncertainty. S2 is ai_vs_human context only.

one_line_finding: Among 844 online volunteers analyzed (3,414 AUT ideas analyzed), seeing ChatGPT example ideas did not change classifier-scored originality (joint F(4, 19.86) = 0.12, p = 0.97; p. 8, Section 5.4; per-arm coefficients in Table 18, p. 26), but both high-exposure conditions raised global idea diversity over the human-examples control (Cliff's delta 0.31 disclosed and 0.26 undisclosed, adjusted p = 0.001; p. 7, Section 5.2; Table 12, p. 22).
open_questions: Text on p. 8 says only [Low Exposure, Undisclosed] had higher global diversity than Control (delta = 0.11, p = 0.001), but Table 12 (p. 22) gives Low Exposure Disclosed - Control = +0.47, delta 0.11, adj p 0.001, and Low Exposure Undisclosed - Control = -0.61, delta -0.06, adj p 0.0063; Figure 7 (p. 7) agrees with the table. The text appears to mislabel the arm; the form follows the table.

The abstract says 'There were no main effects of disclosure', yet Table 12 (p. 22) reports more global diversity when AI ideas were disclosed at both exposure levels (0.41, adj p 0.0328; 1.08, adj p 0.001). The abstract claim may refer only to creativity.

Per-arm participant counts are not reported. Each person can appear in up to five arms (within-person design, 4.05 of 5 trials on average), so n_treatment and n_control for any contrast cannot be read from the paper.

3,414 responses are analyzed (Table 2, SI 3), but the creativity and local-diversity models report 3,271 observations (Tables 18, 14) and the AI-adoption model 2,618 (Table 22); the paper does not explain the difference. Table 9 (p. 20) shows 11 participants with AI feeling missing, and AI feeling enters all three models, so the models may hold fewer than 844 people. Each person gives at most one response per condition, so 3,271 observations imply at least 655 people, and 2,618 AI-condition observations (at most four per person) also imply at least 655.
Comparison type coded ai_vs_active because the control sees six human-written example ideas and the AI arms replace two or four of them; a reviewer may prefer ai_vs_bau.

Whether exposure to pre-generated AI example ideas, with no interaction with the model, counts as generative-AI assistance under criterion 1. Coded met through the codebook's ideas_supplied role ('the study hands participants AI-generated ideas or examples', codebook section 6). The landing page told every participant that some examples came from ChatGPT, and every participant ranked every example (p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 3.4.3), so participants knew the study showed AI ideas and engaged with each example.

Codebook fit of local idea diversity (S1-O5) and AI adoption (S1-O6): each compares one person's idea with the examples shown (S1-O6 with the AI examples only), not different people's outputs with each other. Both are coded construct other and question with_ai, by the codebook rule for outcomes produced with AI available, rather than diversity/across_people.

Primary status: the paper calls only AI adoption secondary. The form codes as paper_primary the three results the abstract names (creativity level, global diversity, evolution of diversity) and leaves the evolution of creativity and local diversity as not_stated.
No participant-level standard error for diversity: global diversity uses Monte Carlo set samples with permutation tests; evolution uses 362 pool-level observations.

Table 1 (p. 7) describes AI adoption as 'maximum semantic distance', but Sections 1.2.2 and 5.5 and SI 10 define it as maximum cosine similarity; Table 1 cites SI 8.3 for local diversity, which is in SI 8.2.

Disclosure: p. 4 says participants 'are not told ideas are from AI', but the study description on the landing page (p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 3.4) told every participant they would see ideas 'even from AI (i.e., ChatGPT)'. So the Disclosed and Undisclosed conditions differ in the per-idea source labels (and, on the Figure 12 screen, a banner), not in whether participants knew the study showed AI ideas. This bears on the ai_design disclosure contrasts, not on the AI-versus-Control contrasts.

Carryover: conditions run in random order within person, so unless Control comes first, a participant's Control trial follows AI trials on other items. The paper's statement that Control ideas are 'clean' from AI contamination (p. 6, Section 3.4.4) refers to the example chains, not to what a participant saw earlier. The local models control for condition order (Tables 14, 18, 22), but the paper reports no first-trial (between-person) contrast.

Not extracted as outcomes: the word-length prompt experiment (Appendix A.2, p. 13; Table 5, p. 17), which compares ChatGPT and human word counts and has no creativity outcome; ranking accuracy and per-trial uniqueness feedback (SI 5, p. 19); moderator contrasts of local diversity (Tables 15-16, p. 24) beyond the main condition test; AI-adoption contrasts by perceived AI creativity (Tables 20-21, pp. 27-28) and the task-difficulty correlation (rho = 0.8 vs 0.3, p. 9, Figure 10, five items). Participant counts by source in Table 3 (p. 8) sum to 844 and trial counts to 3,414. The abstract's '800+ participants, 40+ countries' matches Table 2 (844, 48). No preregistration and no data or code link for this study appear in the document.

open_items.item: Text on p. 8 credits [Low Exposure, Undisclosed] with higher global diversity than Control, but Table 12 (p. 22) and Figure 7 (p. 7) put the gain on Low Exposure, Disclosed. The form follows the table.
The abstract says there were no main effects of disclosure, but Table 12 (p. 22) shows more global diversity in both Disclosed conditions than in the matching Undisclosed ones.

Per-arm counts of people are not reported, so n_treatment and n_control cannot be filled for any contrast. Criterion 2 counts all 844 people analyzed and does not need them. The document names no posted data.

The gap between 3,414 analyzed responses and the 3,271 (creativity, local diversity) and 2,618 (AI adoption) model observations is unexplained, and 11 participants lack AI feeling. The models still hold at least 655 people, so criterion 2 holds either way.

Comparison type for the AI arms against the human-example Control: ai_vs_active or ai_vs_bau. Codebook section 5 and the form-spec note on arms[].ai put human-written examples under other_aid, which gives ai_vs_active.

Whether exposure to pre-generated ChatGPT example ideas, with no interaction with the model, counts as generative-AI assistance (criterion 1). The codebook's ideas_supplied role ('the study hands participants AI-generated ideas or examples') covers it, so criterion 1 stays met.
open_items.scope_note: The item resolves itself: the codebook's ideas_supplied role covers supplied AI ideas, and settled_by is nothing_needed.

open_items.item: Codebook fit of local idea diversity (S1-O5) and AI adoption (S1-O6), both coded other/with_ai because each compares one person's idea with the examples shown. Criterion 3 rests on S1-O1 and S1-O3 in any case.
Primary status: the paper names a status only for AI adoption (secondary) and mentions no preregistration. Codebook section 8 picks the primary record when the paper names none.

No participant-level standard error for the diversity outcomes (Monte Carlo set samples with permutation tests for global diversity, 362 pool-level rows for its evolution). This limits pooling, not eligibility. The document names no posted data.

Table 1 (p. 7) calls AI adoption a maximum semantic distance and cites SI 8.3 for local diversity. Sections 1.2.2 and 5.5 and SI 10 define AI adoption as maximum cosine similarity, and local diversity is in SI 8.2. The form follows the defining sections.

Disclosure: p. 4 says participants are not told ideas are from AI, but the landing page (p. 5, Figure 3) told everyone that some ideas came from ChatGPT. The disclosure factor varies only the per-idea labels, which bears on the ai_design disclosure contrasts.

Carryover: unless Control comes first, a participant's Control trial follows AI trials on other items, and the paper reports no first-trial (between-person) contrast. A within-person design with randomized order meets criterion 1.
The text ends mid-sentence in SI 11.3 (p. 29). The ACM version of record may complete it.
